subChunks.title: Qualitative Research in Psychology: Design, Analysis & Epistemology
subChunks.hookHtml: In 2017, Diana Bailey published a qualitative study exploring how parents of children with autism made sense of their children's diagnosis in the year following it. She didn't use questionnaires or rating scales. She sat with parents and asked them to talk about what it was like — using interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) to understand the experiential and interpretative processes through which people make meaning of significant life events. One parent described the diagnosis as 'like being handed a map for a country you never wanted to visit.' Another said it was 'the day things finally made sense after years of knowing something was different but not having words for it.' These accounts carry knowledge that no standardised scale could capture: the texture of lived experience, the irreducible particularity of how this person, in this life context, is making meaning of this event. Qualitative methods have moved from the margins to the mainstream of psychological research over the past three decades — in health psychology, clinical psychology, educational psychology, and applied social research. They are not a fallback position for researchers who cannot do quantitative work. They are an appropriate and necessary set of methods for specific research questions — particularly those concerned with how people experience, interpret, and make meaning of phenomena. Understanding when and why to use qualitative methods, and how to design and conduct them with appropriate rigour, is a core SENIOR competency for any applied psychologist.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Epistemological Foundation

Qualitative methods rest on different epistemological foundations than quantitative methods — different assumptions about what counts as knowledge and how it is produced:

Positivism: The assumption that there is an objective reality independent of the observer that can be measured and known through rigorous method. Underpins most quantitative research — experiments, surveys, psychometrics — which aims for generalisable, replicable findings about causal relationships.

Interpretivism / constructivism: The assumption that social and psychological reality is constructed through meaning-making — that what matters is not objective behaviour but how people interpret, experience, and give meaning to events. Underpins most qualitative research. Knowledge is context-dependent and the researcher's perspective is part of the knowledge-production process.

Critical realism: A position between positivism and constructivism — accepting that there is a real world independent of our interpretations, but that our access to it is always mediated through interpretation and social context. Allows mixed methods approaches that combine the measurement of real phenomena with attention to how those phenomena are experienced and interpreted.

Understanding these foundations matters because it determines what research questions qualitative methods are appropriate for, and what standards of rigour should be applied to them.

Major Qualitative Methods

Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA; Smith, 1996): Examines how people make sense of their major life experiences — its concern is with experience, meaning, and sense-making from an insider perspective. Typically uses in-depth semi-structured interviews with small, purposively sampled groups (often 6–10 participants). Analysis involves detailed line-by-line annotation, identification of experiential themes, clustering into super-ordinate themes, and writing accounts that balance close interpretation with the participant's own voice. IPA is idiographic (detailed accounts of individuals) before nomothetic (patterns across participants).

Thematic Analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006): A flexible method for identifying, analysing, and reporting patterns (themes) within qualitative data. Unlike IPA, thematic analysis is not committed to a specific philosophical orientation and can be used inductively (themes driven by data) or deductively (themes driven by theory). Braun and Clarke distinguish reflexive thematic analysis (themes are interpretive constructs of the researcher, not objective units extracted from data) from poorly specified uses of 'thematic analysis' as a grab-bag method. The most widely used qualitative method in psychology.

Grounded Theory (Glaser & Strauss, 1967; Charmaz, 2006): An iterative, systematic method for generating theory grounded in data. Uses theoretical sampling (sampling decisions guided by emerging theory), constant comparison (comparing incidents and categories as they emerge), and saturation (sampling until no new theoretical insights emerge). Particularly suited to generating explanatory accounts of social processes rather than describing experience.

Discourse Analysis / Conversation Analysis: Analysis of language as a social act — how talk performs social functions, constructs identities, and produces social reality. Conversation analysis (CA) examines the fine-grained structure of naturally occurring interaction (turn-taking, repair, sequence organisation). Discourse analysis (DA) examines how language constructs meaning at a broader level.

Narrative Analysis: Studies how people construct and tell stories about their lives and experiences. Narrative is understood as a fundamental human sense-making activity; the structure, content, and form of personal narratives reveals how people construct identity and make meaning of difficult events.

Rigour in Qualitative Research

Qualitative research does not aim for statistical reliability and generalisability in the quantitative sense. Alternative quality criteria:

Credibility     — (equivalent to validity) — are the findings
                  plausible and well-grounded in data? Member
                  checking, thick description, negative case
                  analysis

Transferability — (equivalent to external validity) — can readers
                  assess whether findings might apply to their
                  context? Achieved through thick description
                  of the research context and participants

Dependability   — (equivalent to reliability) — would another
                  researcher following the same process reach
                  similar conclusions? Audit trail of analytic
                  decisions

Confirmability  — (equivalent to objectivity) — are findings
                  grounded in data rather than researcher
                  projection? Reflexivity statement, inter-rater
                  discussion

Reflexivity is particularly important: qualitative researchers must actively examine and report how their own background, assumptions, and position shape the research process and interpretations. This is not a contamination to be eliminated (as in quantitative research) but an acknowledged feature of knowledge production to be managed and reported.

When Qualitative Methods Are Appropriate

Qualitative methods are specifically appropriate for research questions that ask:

  • How do people experience [phenomenon]? (phenomenological questions)
  • What meanings do people make of [event or experience]? (interpretive questions)
  • What processes underlie [social phenomenon]? (grounded theory questions)
  • How is [identity/role/practice] constructed through language? (discursive questions)

They are less appropriate for: estimating prevalence, testing causal hypotheses, or generalising findings statistically to populations. Rigorous mixed methods designs can combine both — using qualitative methods to understand experience and process, and quantitative methods to test prevalence and causation.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen distributes a transcript of an interview excerpt — one paragraph, about 200 words — from an IPA study on living with chronic pain. She asks students to work in pairs and annotate what they notice. Three minutes later, she asks what they found. Every pair has noticed different things.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The fact that you noticed different things is not a problem — it's a feature. Qualitative analysis is not about extracting the single correct reading from the data. It is about producing a rigorous, systematically derived, well-evidenced interpretation — one interpretation among others that could have been made — and being transparent about the process through which it was made. Reflexivity and audit trail are not post-hoc additions. They are the primary evidence that the researcher has been rigorous.

storyBeats.speaker: IPA in health psychology
storyBeats.text: Leukaemia patients in a 2016 IPA study by Rodriguez et al. described a specific paradox in their experience of remission: the end of active treatment — which should feel like relief — was experienced as profoundly frightening, because treatment had provided structure, medical contact, and a sense of being 'actively fought for.' Remission left them without the scaffolding that had organised their experience of illness. This finding — which emerged from patients' own accounts of their meaning-making — would not have been detectable through a questionnaire on anxiety or quality of life. The quantitative data showed improvement in outcomes at remission; the qualitative data showed a complex, paradoxical experience that explained why many patients found remission psychologically harder than they expected. Both levels of analysis were necessary.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The most important skill in qualitative analysis is the capacity to hold your data lightly — to stay with the text, let it challenge your assumptions, look for what doesn't fit your emerging interpretation, and be prepared to revise. The common failure in qualitative research is confirmation bias dressed up as analysis: finding the themes you expected to find because that's what you were looking for. Negative case analysis — actively seeking data that doesn't fit — is the primary methodological defence against this.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A clinical psychologist is designing a research study to explore how adult survivors of childhood sexual abuse experience the process of disclosing their history for the first time in a therapeutic context. They are deciding between: (A) a survey study using standardised questionnaires measuring psychological wellbeing, shame, and therapeutic alliance, with 200 participants; and (B) an IPA study using in-depth semi-structured interviews with 8 participants who have recently made a first disclosure in therapy.

  1. What different research questions could each design answer, and why is one more appropriate than the other for the stated research aim?
  2. What specific ethical considerations apply to qualitative research with this population that might not be salient in quantitative survey research?
  3. Describe what 'reflexivity' requires of the researcher in this study, and why it is particularly important given the topic area.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Different research questions and appropriateness: Design A (survey/quantitative) is appropriate for questions such as: What is the prevalence of specific psychological outcomes (shame, wellbeing, therapeutic alliance strength) in adult survivors who have made first disclosures in therapy? Does therapeutic alliance predict better outcomes following first disclosure? Are certain demographic or trauma-related factors associated with disclosure outcomes? — Questions about prevalence, relationships between variables, and generalisation to populations. Design B (IPA/qualitative) is appropriate for questions such as: How do adult survivors experience and make sense of the process of first disclosure in a therapeutic context? What meanings do they attach to the experience? What are the moment-by-moment phenomenological dimensions of making a disclosure — what it feels like, what it means, what it changes? The stated research aim — exploring how survivors experience first disclosure — is inherently a phenomenological, meaning-focused question. It asks about subjective experience and sense-making, not about prevalence or variable relationships. Design B (IPA) is therefore more appropriate for the stated aim. Design A would produce important contextual data but would not address the 'how do people experience' question. Neither design is inherently superior — they address different questions; the key is matching design to aim.

2. Ethical considerations specific to qualitative research with this population: (a) Risk of re-traumatisation: In-depth, unstructured interview exploration of disclosure experiences requires careful attention to the risk that participants are re-exposed to traumatic material without adequate support. Unlike standardised questionnaires (which can be completed at the participant's own pace and stopped), interview contexts create interpersonal pressure that may make it harder for participants to disengage. The researcher must: screen participants for current stability, provide clear information about what the interview will involve and the right to stop at any time, have a protocol for responding if participants become distressed during the interview (including referral pathways), and provide an aftercare debrief. (b) Dual role management: If the researcher is also a clinician, there is a risk of role confusion (participant begins treating the interview as a therapeutic session). This should be explicitly discussed in the information sheet and at the start of the interview. (c) Informed consent as ongoing process: Unlike one-time questionnaire consent, qualitative interview consent should be understood as a process — participants have the right to withdraw data after the interview when they have had more time to reflect on what they have shared. (d) Confidentiality limits: Particularly important in research involving abuse disclosures — the researcher must be clear about confidentiality limits (safeguarding obligations if current risk is disclosed) and communicate these at consent stage.

3. Reflexivity requirements: Reflexivity in qualitative research requires the researcher to actively examine and report how their own background, assumptions, positioning, and emotional responses shape the research process and interpretations. In this study, reflexivity is particularly important because: (a) The researcher may have personal or professional experience with sexual abuse disclosure (as a therapist, a survivor, or both), which will shape what they attend to in the data, how they establish rapport in interviews, what they find emotionally difficult, and what interpretations feel 'obvious' to them. These are not disqualifying factors, but they must be examined and reported. (b) The topic carries significant social, political, and moral weight — prevailing cultural narratives about abuse (victims should speak out; disclosure is always beneficial; therapeutic disclosure is a healing process) may shape the researcher's expectation of what they will find and what themes 'matter.' These assumptions can bias analysis toward expected findings. (c) Power dynamics in the interview — the researcher is positioned as expert; participants may feel pressure to provide 'useful' or 'valid' accounts. The researcher's awareness of this power differential and how they manage it (e.g., through collaborative member-checking) should be reported. Reflexivity should be documented throughout the research process in a reflexive journal, not only in the write-up.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A quantitatively-oriented psychologist colleague argues: 'Qualitative research is not really scientific — it produces subjective interpretations that cannot be verified, replicated, or generalised. It should not be published in peer-reviewed journals or used to inform clinical practice.' Critically evaluate this argument, drawing on the epistemological foundations of qualitative research and its quality criteria. Aim for 250–300 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The colleague's argument misapplies quantitative standards of rigour to a different epistemological tradition — conflating 'scientific' with 'quantitative.' This is a category error: science is characterised by systematic inquiry, transparency, and accountability to evidence, not by any specific method. Qualitative methods can meet these criteria on their own terms.

The accusation of subjectivity misunderstands both qualitative and quantitative research. All research involves interpretive choices — in hypothesis selection, operationalisation, statistical model choice, and interpretation of results. Quantitative research manages this through standardisation and statistical correction; qualitative research manages it through rigorous analytic procedures (systematic coding, negative case analysis, audit trail) and reflexivity. The difference is in how interpretation is managed, not whether interpretation occurs.

The 'cannot be verified' claim fails to engage with qualitative quality criteria. Credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability provide methodological standards appropriate to qualitative research's aims. Member checking, thick description, and audit trails serve parallel functions to quantitative reliability and validity checks. Qualitative findings from well-designed studies do replicate in the relevant sense — common experiential patterns re-emerge across multiple studies of similar populations and phenomena.

The 'cannot be generalised' point correctly identifies that qualitative research does not aim for statistical generalisation to populations. But it aims for analytic generalisation — the generalisability of theoretical insights across contexts — which is a legitimate and valuable form of knowledge. Findings from IPA studies on chronic pain experience, for example, have informed clinical practice guidelines by illuminating processes and experiences that questionnaires cannot capture.

Qualitative and quantitative methods address different research questions. A field that excluded qualitative research would be impoverished — systematically unable to understand the subjective, experiential, and meaning-making dimensions of human psychology.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what makes qualitative research different from a survey study — and give a concrete example of a question that you could only really answer by actually talking in depth with a small number of people.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Smith's (1996) qualitative method examining how people make sense of major life experiences. Uses in-depth semi-structured interviews with small purposive samples; produces detailed idiographic accounts of experience before nomothetic analysis of patterns across cases. Central to health, clinical, and educational psychology research.

The qualitative researcher's systematic examination of how their own background, assumptions, position, and emotional responses shape the research process and interpretations. Not a contamination to eliminate but an acknowledged, managed, and reported feature of knowledge production in interpretive research.

Glaser and Strauss's (1967) iterative qualitative method for generating theory grounded in data. Uses theoretical sampling, constant comparison, and theoretical saturation. Produces explanatory accounts of social processes rather than descriptions of experience. Multiple versions (classic, Straussian, constructivist-Charmaz) vary in epistemological assumptions.

A qualitative rigour strategy involving actively searching for data that contradicts or challenges emerging interpretations. Provides a check against confirmation bias in qualitative analysis — interpretations that survive scrutiny of disconfirming evidence are more credible.

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary focus of Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA)?
options: Statistical analysis of large survey datasets to identify psychological patterns
How people make sense of and experience major life events — from an insider, meaning-focused perspective
Generating hypothesis-testing experiments from observations of natural language
Analysing the frequency of specific language patterns in texts
questions.correctAnswer: How people make sense of and experience major life events — from an insider, meaning-focused perspective
questions.explanationHtml: IPA (Smith, 1996) is a qualitative method with a dual focus: phenomenological (concerned with experience as lived from the inside — texture, meaning, embodied quality) and interpretative (recognising that access to experience is always interpretative, both for the participant making sense of their experience and for the researcher making sense of the participant's account). It typically uses in-depth semi-structured interviews with small, purposively sampled groups, aiming for rich, detailed understanding of how specific individuals experience specific phenomena rather than statistical generalisation across populations. It is particularly widely used in health psychology, clinical psychology, and counselling psychology research on illness, significant life transitions, and identity.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: In qualitative research, the researcher's subjectivity and personal background are contaminants that should be eliminated through rigorous methodology, as in quantitative research.
questions.explanationHtml: False. In qualitative research, particularly in interpretive and constructivist traditions, the researcher is not a neutral instrument but an active participant in knowledge production whose perspective inevitably shapes what is noticed, how data are interpreted, and what conclusions are reached. Rather than attempting to eliminate this (which is impossible and would misrepresent the epistemological reality), qualitative research manages it through reflexivity — systematically examining, reporting, and accounting for how the researcher's position shapes the research. This is an epistemological commitment, not a methodological failure. In quantitative research, standardisation aims to reduce researcher influence; in qualitative research, reflexivity makes researcher influence transparent and accountable. Both are legitimate approaches to managing the challenge of knowledge production — they reflect different epistemological assumptions about what objectivity means and whether it is achievable.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher conducts an IPA study on the experience of being made redundant, interviewing 8 participants. A reviewer says 'The sample of 8 is too small — the findings cannot be generalised and therefore the study is invalid.' How should the researcher respond?
options: Agree — IPA studies should always use samples of at least 50 to be generalisable

Explain that IPA does not aim for statistical generalisation to populations; a sample of 6–10 is appropriate for the method; validity is assessed through credibility and transferability criteria rather than sample size
Acknowledge the limitation and rerun the study with a larger sample using thematic analysis instead
Argue that sample size is irrelevant in all qualitative research
questions.correctAnswer: Explain that IPA does not aim for statistical generalisation to populations; a sample of 6–10 is appropriate for the method; validity is assessed through credibility and transferability criteria rather than sample size
questions.explanationHtml: The reviewer's criticism applies quantitative sampling logic to a qualitative method — a methodological category error. IPA does not aim for statistical generalisation to populations (the stated goal of quantitative sampling); it aims for analytic generalisation — theoretically meaningful insights grounded in detailed, credible accounts. Smith's IPA guidelines recommend samples of 3–6 for doctoral research and 6–10 for journal articles — small by quantitative standards but appropriate for the depth of analysis required. Larger samples in IPA produce analytically unmanageable data and often result in superficial 'thematic' analysis rather than the fine-grained, idiographic analysis IPA requires. The appropriate quality criteria for IPA are credibility (are findings well-grounded in data?), transferability (does thick description allow assessment of applicability?), and confirmability (are conclusions evidenced rather than projected?) — none of which require large samples. The researcher should educate the reviewer about the appropriate epistemological framework for evaluating qualitative research.
